architecture.mechanism: Direct in-line pressure sensing of the infusion set against a calibrated occlusion threshold (20 Psi per ECRI), where a water pressure sensor detects rising upstream pressure caused by a downstream blockage and transmits the signal to a processor for real-time evaluation, with calibration accuracy quantified per device (error margins 2.84%–71.26%).
architecture.intervention: Integrate a periodically recalibrated (annual, per ECRI 20 Psi benchmark) in-line pressure sensor upstream of the patient connection whose output is continuously compared against a calibrated occlusion threshold by the pump's processor; on threshold crossing, immediately halt the pumping mechanism and trigger the occlusion alarm, with per-unit sensor error verified during calibration so the effective alarm threshold is derated by the measured sensor error margin.
architecture.expected_effect: Occlusion-induced pressure rise is detected at the sensor before the delivered volume/pressure deviation propagates to the patient, enabling alarm and pump stoppage prior to harmful medication or fluid delivery deviation; routine calibration against a dual-channel analyzer keeps sensor drift (up to ~71% error observed in uncalibrated devices) from delaying or masking detection.
architecture.falsification_test: Bench test with a syringe pump infusing water at clinical rates (e.g., 5–100 mL/h) through a test set with a programmable downstream resistance (solenoid valve or clamp) creating gradual occlusion; measure time from occlusion onset to alarm and delivered-volume deviation at alarm, before and after sensor calibration. The mechanism is falsified if any calibrated unit alarms only after pressure/volume deviation exceeds the harmful threshold, or if post-calibration sensor error exceeds the derating allowance (e.g., >5%).

thirty_year_engine.current: Passive, threshold-based in-line pressure sensing — a single static occlusion threshold (20 Psi) compared against a periodically calibrated sensor, with alarm only after pressure has already risen past the derated threshold; the pump is an open-loop deliverer with a passive watchdog.
thirty_year_engine.evolution_2055: By 2055 infusion delivery is fully closed-loop: pumps continuously identify the patient-line hydraulic plant (resistance, compliance) via active micro-perturbations, predict occlusion onset from parameter drift rather than absolute pressure, and autonomously re-regulate flow to hold delivered-dose fidelity — the vasopressor closed-loop and automated insulin delivery pattern generalized to fluid/medication infusion.
thirty_year_engine.required_capability: The diagnosis (obvious_combination kill) shows the parent lacks any non-obvious causal capability: it cannot detect occlusion before pressure crosses a threshold, cannot distinguish true downstream blockage from benign compliance changes, and cannot actuate anything other than stop-and-alarm. What is missing is predictive, model-based detection and active regulation — not better calibration of the same passive sensor.
thirty_year_engine.capability_backcast: 2055: fully predictive closed-loop infusion with self-identifying hydraulic models. 2040: embedded micro-perturbation flow probes with on-pump system identification; occlusion predicted minutes ahead. 2030: motor-current/torque signatures fused with pressure for early occlusion inference (already nascent in peristaltic pump literature). 2025: closed-loop vasopressor and AID systems demonstrate embedded plant identification and failure-mode-aware control in clinical software; cheap high-resolution motor encoders and current sensing on pumps.
thirty_year_engine.todays_frontier: Closed-loop control architectures from clinical automation — specifically closed-loop vasopressor systems and automated insulin delivery (twiist), where the controller continuously identifies the controlled plant's response characteristics and detects actuator/sensor failure modes from model residual drift rather than from fixed alarm thresholds.
thirty_year_engine.transfer: Import the closed-loop "identify-then-predict" regime from vasopressor/AID control into the infusion pump: instead of passively watching one pressure number, the pump actively probes the line with sub-clinical flow micro-perturbations, fits a hydraulic resistance/compliance model, and detects occlusion as a statistically significant drift in identified plant parameters — hours-to-minutes before any static pressure threshold would trip.
